bibliography.abstract: Abstract Transit users are considered insensitive to fare changes. Therefore, reducing fares is often viewed as ineffective for increasing ridership. However, removing fares has led to markedly different outcomes in practice. Fare-free transit (FFT) policies have resulted in substantial increases in ridership among the agencies that implemented them. This contrast between expected behavior and actual FFT outcomes suggests a gap between theoretical fare elasticities and the actual sensitivity of transit users in the FFT context. This study examines sensitivity to fare and service changes among FFT users, using 2024 survey data from five U.S. transit agencies. Four cumulative linked mixed models are applied, one for each of fare, in-vehicle time, waiting time, and walking time. Results reveal that riders are far more responsive to fare reinstatement than previously thought, with a 7.6 times greater likelihood of decreasing ridership per dollar increased in fare. Riders also respond more strongly to fare reinstatement than to travel time increases: a $1 reinstated fare was perceived equally as a ~ 20-min increase in travel time, while a $2 fare was perceived on par with an additional 35-min travel time. This research also examines the potential impacts of reinstating fares after operating fare-free for a while, and indicates that it could cause sharp ridership declines: 50% of new users in our sample could stop riding if fares exceed $1.30, and an overall 50% ridership loss is expected for the sample agencies if fares rise above $1.90. The study also provides key insights and recommendations for agencies considering the implementation or reversal of FFT policies.
bibliography.title: Fare sensitivity at point zero: How fare-free transit riders react to fare reinstatement and service changes?

en.caveats: Findings rely on self-reported survey responses regarding hypothetical fare reinstatements rather than observed behavioral card-swipe data.
en.what: Analyzing 2024 survey data from five US transit agencies using four cumulative linked mixed models, this study measures how fare-free transit users react to fare reinstatements and service alterations. Riders are 7.6 times more likely to reduce transit use for each dollar increase in fare, valuing a $1 reinstated fare equivalent to roughly a 20-minute travel time increase, and a $2 fare equivalent to 35 minutes. Reintroducing fares above $1.30 risks losing 50% of new users, while fares exceeding $1.90 predict a 50% drop in total ridership across the studied systems.
en.why: This refutes the common assumption that transit riders are insensitive to fare changes, showing that removing and then reinstating fares creates far higher fare sensitivity than standard elasticity models predict.
